strengths: Novel application of affordance-aware textual descriptions to 3D hand reconstruction, extending beyond categorical labels to capture rich object properties, interactions, and intentions
Well-motivated two-step description generation pipeline using chain-of-thought reasoning (VLM parsing followed by LLM summarization) that improves upon naive direct captioning
Consistent experimental improvements across all occlusion levels, with substantial 25% error reduction under heavy occlusion (4.9mm), addressing a practically important scenario
Principled approach to occlusion detection combining ray-casting for self-occlusion and SAM2 masking for object-occlusion, with targeted refinement of only uncertain joints
Clear presentation with effective visualizations; good demonstration of controllability showing the model responds to affordance variations (Figure 5)
Practical focus on severe occlusion scenarios relevant to VR/AR and robotic manipulation applications
weaknesses: Critical dependency on ground truth grasp taxonomy from HOGraspNet rather than predicting it with the VLM, directly undermining the claim of using VLMs for rich contextual knowledge. Grasp taxonomy classification is acknowledged as 'highly challenging' but no solution is proposed, creating a significant gap between the stated contribution and actual implementation

Limited evaluation scope: single-dataset evaluation (HOGraspNet only) without cross-dataset validation; only 1/10 of dataset used (~150k images); evaluation on only 300 instances in Table 1. Raises concerns about generalization beyond this specific benchmark

Modest average improvement of only 0.23mm across all occlusion levels (8.51→8.28mm), with negligible gains at low occlusion (7.69→7.67mm). Significant improvements concentrate in high-occlusion regime, limiting general applicability

Missing critical ablation studies: (1) two-step description vs. direct generation, (2) individual affordance element contributions (which matters most?), (3) refinement strategy components, (4) sensitivity to description quality. These ablations are essential to validate design choices

Insufficient baseline comparisons: only HaMeR and a weakened InterHandGen variant without text conditioning. No comparison with other context-aware, semantic, or affordance-based hand pose estimation methods. The unexplained degradation of unconditional InterHandGen at low occlusion deserves investigation

Incomplete training details and reproducibility concerns: sparse descriptions of diffusion model training (dataset composition, loss functions, hyperparameters), no discussion of computational costs, no mention of code availability, no quantification of VLM/LLM inference overhead at test time

VLM robustness not analyzed: no evaluation of sensitivity to VLM description errors, no comparison of different VLMs or prompts, no analysis of error propagation from VLM through the pipeline. Heavy reliance on off-the-shelf QwenVL2.5 and Mistral-7B without validation

Limited technical novelty: diffusion architecture adapted from InterHandGen [12], refinement strategy from prior work [16], uses off-the-shelf VLM/LLM/CLIP components. Primary novelty is in application combination rather than methodological innovation

Generalization concerns: SAM2-based object-occlusion detection may not transfer across datasets; no evaluation with different hand pose initializers, object categories, or camera views beyond HOGraspNet; all experiments use HaMeR as sole baseline estimator

No failure case analysis or discussion of when affordance guidance might conflict with visual evidence; no investigation of failure modes or failure rate; qualitative analysis limited to cherry-picked examples and narrow affordance variations (object size only)
